title: Old-Time Hay Box Cooking
subtitle: The Fireless Cooker of 1916
items: Use a heavy pot, tight lid
Nest it in hay, wool or quilts
Don't open it while it cooks
intro: A century ago, USDA Farmers' Bulletin 771 taught families to finish cooking in a "fireless cooker": an insulated box that holds a pot's heat for hours. It saves fuel and still works when the power is out. Here is the method in our own words.
desc: Old-time hay box cooking, the fireless cooker from a 1916 USDA bulletin: bring oatmeal, beans or stew to a hard boil, nest the covered pot in hay, wool or quilts, and let stored heat finish the cooking with no fuel. Handy for power outages and off-grid living. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Can Pickled Beets
subtitle: USDA-Tested Water Bath Method
intro: Plain beets are low-acid and need a pressure canner, but pickled beets have enough vinegar to be safely processed in a boiling water bath. These steps follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.
desc: How to can pickled beets the USDA-tested way: leave stems and roots on while cooking so color stays in, slip the skins, slice, cover with a 5% vinegar brine, leave 1/2-inch headspace and process pints or quarts 30 minutes in a boiling water bath, adjusting for altitude. Full list on the blog.

title: Winter Fruit Tree Pruning Basics
subtitle: Prune While Trees Are Dormant
items: Cut dead and broken wood first
Take no more than 1/4 a year
desc: Winter fruit tree pruning basics for beginners: prune apple and pear trees while dormant in late winter, use sharp clean bypass pruners, remove dead, broken and crossing branches first and cut just outside the branch collar. See the tools you need. (Contains affiliate links.)

title: Winter Care for Asparagus Beds
subtitle: Set Up Next Spring's Harvest
items: Weed the bed one last time
Spread 2 in. of compost on top
Mark rows so no one digs them
No harvest in a bed's 1st year
intro: An asparagus bed can produce for 15 years or more, and a little care in late fall pays off every spring. Cutting the old ferns also removes places where asparagus beetles spend the winter.
desc: Winter care for asparagus beds: cut back the brown ferns after frost, weed, top-dress with compost and mulch 4-6 inches of straw or shredded leaves so the crowns come back strong next spring. Full list on the blog.

title: How to Freeze Kale & Greens
subtitle: Blanch, Chill, Pack
intro: Kale, chard, spinach and other greens freeze well if you blanch them first. Blanching stops the enzymes that make frozen greens tough and off-flavored, and frozen greens drop straight into soups and smoothies.
desc: How to freeze kale, spinach, chard and other greens: wash, trim tough stems, blanch 2 minutes (collards 3), cool in ice water, drain and pack tightly in freezer bags for winter soups and smoothies. Full list on the blog.

title: Keep Winter Eggs From Freezing
subtitle: Cold-Weather Egg Collecting
intro: On freezing days an egg can freeze and crack within a few hours of being laid. A few small habits keep your backyard eggs safe and clean all winter.
desc: How to keep backyard chicken eggs from freezing in winter: collect eggs two or three times a day, throw out any that froze and cracked, add deep bedding and curtains to nest boxes and block drafts while keeping the coop vented. Full list on the blog.
